newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees more cooperation in fight against drugs.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees more cooperation in fight against drugs.

text.p: EU justice ministers agreed after a heated debate on Friday to co-operate better in the fight against drug addiction and trafficking, an issue which has long opposed the Netherlands to its 14 partners.

The compromise struck by the ministers says European Union states "can maintain or introduce more efficient measures" to control drugs -- leaving the Dutch free to allow coffee-shops, where soft drugs such as cannabis are currently widely available, to continue trading.
But French and Dutch officials will be able, if they want, to pool efforts to fight trafficking.
"We have reached a broad agreement on the text presented by the French. It represents a major step forward," Irish Justice Minister Nora Owen told a news conference after the meeting.
Earlier on Friday, French Justice Minister Jacques Toubon threatened to take the issue to the summit of EU heads of state and government in Dublin next month.
"(French President Jacques) Chirac is determined to have this question discussed at the European Council," he told reporters.

This followed an attempt by Dutch Justice Minister Winnie Sorgdrager to impose a much toned down version of the text, which would have removed the accent from fighting drug addiction and given approval to Dutch drugs policy.

This was unequivocally rejected by its partners. "There was an attempt made by the Netherlands to water this joint action. That attempt failed," British Home Affairs Minister Michael Howard told a news briefing.
Justice and police matters are still to a large extent the responsbility of national governments, which means that any decision to harmonise laws must be taken unanimously.
France, eager to fight an increase in "drug tourism" to the Netherlands since the abolition of the EU's internal borders in 1994, wants to align national laws on fighting drug use and trafficking.
But French diplomats played down the suggestion that they were trying to blose the Dutch coffee-shops.
"There is a big misunderstanding regarding the expression 'fight against drug addiction'," one said. "That does not mean we want to ban soft drugs."
